title: Narada's Farewell
on_slide_text: After hearing Narada's tale of the perfect man, Valmiki worshipped him with his disciples and bowed in gratitude. Honoured, Narada blessed them and rose through the sky to his own realm, leaving the sage by the Ganga where a tiny sight would soon birth a deathless epic.
rationale: Opens on the hook after Narada's blessing, showing his skyward departure that sets up the tiny incident about to birth the epic.

title: The Pure Tamasa Ghat
on_slide_text: Valmiki walked to the Tamasa river near the Ganga and found a holy bathing spot, clear, beautiful, and free of mud. Pleased, he called to his disciple, Child Bharadwaja, set down the pitcher and hand me my bark cloth, for I will bathe here.
rationale: Establishes the mud-free holy spot and Valmiki's request for bark cloth, the calm before the transformative sight.

title: Clear Water, Clear Mind
question: Why is Tamasa's mud-free ghat compared to the mind of good men just before the killing?
answer: Layer one: the simile is condition, not decoration, for reflection needs still water. Layer two: Valmiki sought purity for bathing but gained purity of seeing, so he heard both play and scream. Layer three: city minds filled with noise witness daily killings unmoved, proving sensitivity is cleanliness before morality. Practice: take ten screen-free quiet minutes daily to let inner mud settle.
on_slide_text: Why compare the clear ghat to a good mind? Because purity is not decoration but condition for seeing; as still water reflects, a noise-free mind perceives another's pain, letting Valmiki hear both play and scream, teaching us to settle inner mud daily to truly notice suffering.
rationale: Pauses on the pure-ghat simile to explain why inner clarity must precede compassion.

title: Song of the Kraunchas
on_slide_text: Before bathing, Valmiki wandered through the riverside forest, looking around in peace. Near a tree he saw two krauncha birds, mates in joyful love-play, singing sweetly to each other. Their happy music filled the clear air, untouched by fear or sorrow.
rationale: Presents the joyful pair in love-play, the image of love whose loss will trigger the epic.

title: Arrow Without Hatred
on_slide_text: In that very moment of song, a cruel Nishada fowler crept near and, without hatred or cause, aimed his arrow at the loving pair. The shaft struck the male krauncha, who fell drenched in blood, writhing in pain while his mate screamed in sudden, helpless grief.
rationale: Isolates the killing without enmity as its own beat, preserving the shock of celebration shattered.

title: Violence Against Joy
question: The fowler was only doing his daily work, so why did Valmiki condemn a killing without enmity as grave adharma?
answer: Layer one: the key qualifier is without cause, without hatred; Valmiki does not oppose food but shattering love absorbed in play. Layer two: the male died not in battle but while singing and loving, violence aimed at celebration itself. Layer three: this mirrors today when boredom, views or profit make us shoot arrows through mockery, interruption or trolling. Practice: notice where you become Nishada and choose silence.
on_slide_text: If the fowler only worked for food, why call it grave sin? Because he killed without cause or hatred, shattering love in its play, striking celebration itself, not battle. His curse mirrors us today when boredom or profit makes us loose arrows into others' joy, urging silence instead.
rationale: Reflects on causeless violence to show why shattering play is adharma, not mere livelihood.

title: The Curse of Compassion
speaker: Valmiki
on_slide_text: O Nishada fowler, you have cruelly killed one innocent krauncha lost in love and sweet song without cause! Therefore you shall never find honour or peace in this world; your name shall bear this injustice as long as living beings remember love torn apart by needless violence.
rationale: Gives the curse its own panel as the emotional climax where compassion erupts as anger.

title: Shoka Becomes Shloka
question: Why does the great epic begin not with a blessing but with a curse, and why is compassion first heard in anger?
answer: Layer one: shoka and shloka share one root, when sorrow overflows it bursts as rhythm. Layer two: rage is not justice but soul's cry at loss of love; anger is compassion boiling over. Layer three: psychology agrees formless pain becomes trauma while rhythmic pain becomes meaning, so lament bound in metre turned immortal. Hence Ramayana starts with separation, not war. Practice: give sharp grief four rhythmic lines.
on_slide_text: Why does eternity open with a curse, not a blessing? Because shoka becomes shloka when overflowing sorrow finds rhythm; Valmiki's anger is compassion boiling over at severed love, proving formless pain wounds while measured lament heals, so the epic rightly starts with separation, not war.
rationale: Unpacks why a curse births poetry, linking sorrow, anger and rhythm to the epic's start in separation.

slide_label: Slide09 - What Came From My Mouth
title: What Came From My Mouth
speaker: Valmiki
on_slide_text: What words have just come from my mouth in grief? Look, disciple, this sentence falls in equal feet and rhythm, fit to be sung to the veena! Born of my sorrow, my shoka, it shall henceforth be called shloka, the first verse of poetry.
rationale: Holds Valmiki's startled recognition separate, marking the conscious discovery of metre from sorrow.

title: Creation Before Understanding
question: Why does the wise Valmiki startle at his own utterance and ask, what has come from my mouth?
answer: Layer one: most human moment, true creation happens first and understanding follows. Layer two: he did not construct equal feet and syllables fit for veena; compassion's natural music settled on its own, what we call flow where unconscious outruns conscious. Layer three: he at once makes the disciple witness, for the first spark needs a second pair of eyes to survive. Practice: write down true lines at once and share with someone trusted.
on_slide_text: Why does the sage startle at his own lips? Because true creation flows before understanding; grief itself shaped equal syllables fit for veena, not grammar but compassion's music, the unconscious outrunning thought. So he calls his disciple to witness, for a newborn spark needs trusted eyes to survive.
rationale: Explores flow and witness, why the sage needs Bharadwaja to confirm the unplanned creation.

title: Bathing With the Verse
on_slide_text: His disciple Bharadwaja joyfully affirmed the new metre, giving Valmiki quiet satisfaction. The sage then bathed in the holy Tamasa waters and walked back to the hermitage, turning the verse over in his mind, while Bharadwaja followed behind bearing the filled water pitcher.
rationale: Covers the bathing and brooding return, bridging the riverbank discovery to the hermitage revelation.

title: Brahma Arrives
on_slide_text: At the hermitage Valmiki spoke of ordinary things, yet the sorrowful metre echoed endlessly within him. Then to everyone's wonder, the radiant four-faced Lord Brahma himself appeared in splendour, come in person to meet the musing sage.
rationale: Introduces Brahma's astonishing arrival while Valmiki remains inwardly fixed on the verse.

title: Worship of the Creator
on_slide_text: The moment he saw the Creator, Valmiki rose in awe and stood silent with folded hands. He bowed low, offered water to wash Brahma's feet, gave him the honoured seat and worshipped him duly, while Brahma kindly asked his welfare and bade him sit.
rationale: Shows due worship and welcome, pausing before divine instruction while grief still lingers.

title: Compose Rama's Story
speaker: Brahma
on_slide_text: Do not doubt, for this metre from your grieving lips shall be immortal by My will alone. Now compose Rama's whole story in this same shloka — all you heard from Narada and more, of Rama, Lakshmana, Sita and the rakshasas. Even the unknown shall be revealed, and no word of yours shall prove false.
rationale: Delivers Brahma's central command and boons of revelation and truth, turning private grief toward Ramayana.

title: Wound Into Work
question: Why does Brahma snatch Valmiki's private grief and order him to make it the vast tale of Rama, Sita and the rakshasas?
answer: Layer one: Brahma converts wound into work; lonely sorrow stays lament but acknowledged sorrow becomes resolve for every separated Sita. Layer two: by my will it burst forth reframes suffering as divine design, not punishment. Layer three: boons that even the unknown will be seen and no word false prove compassion sees larger truth than fact, outlasting mountains. Practice: name one old hurt and turn it to serve someone.
on_slide_text: Why turn one bird's death into Rama's epic? Because Brahma converts wound into work; private lament becomes resolve for every separated Sita when suffering is seen as design, not punishment. Compassion reveals deeper truth than fact, so a grief-song blessed by heaven can outlast mountains and oceans.
rationale: Reframes divine intervention as turning personal wound into universal blessing and enduring truth.

title: The Disciples Sing
on_slide_text: Promising that his Ramayana would live as long as mountains and oceans endure, and that Valmiki would dwell in both Brahma's world and this world while it is sung, Brahma vanished. Amazed, the disciples sang the four-part shloka again and again in deep pathos.
rationale: Captures Brahma's vanishing and the disciples' joyful repetition, confirming the metre will carry the epic.

title: Birth of the Ramayana
on_slide_text: Thus blessed, the graceful sage Valmiki bound Rama's dynasty in hundreds of sweet, melodious shlokas. Hear the life of Rama, noblest of Raghus, and the fall of ten-headed Ravana, told in simple rhythmic words. Here, from sorrow's verse, the deathless Ramayana is born.
rationale: Closes on the resolving beat where sorrow becomes scripture, announcing the Ramayana's birth.
